headline: Scheduled work is a fixed floor today, not yet a load. Supabase calls the app 13,250 times a day and those calls send about 170,000 statements, almost all finding nothing because the platform is not open; in database time that is seconds to a few minutes a day. An empty table is not a finding, so nothing here argues for removing, parking or hiding a feature. Three things are real. (1) Measured waste: pg_cron's own run log is never pruned and is 564 MB, 77% of the 731 MB database, growing with every scheduled call. (2) Timing: six of the nine every-minute routes have a true queue and could be called only when a row waits, and about 30 of the 83 five-minute jobs do daily or hourly work. (3) The one that matters at opening: several jobs do work per store, per page or per order on every run whether or not anything changed (chat knowledge re-reads every page, media and alt texts loop over every store, embeddings hash every product, automations query each store each minute, ad conversions re-offer a week of orders each minute, the cookie scan's due check reads every site, failing scans and waiting invoices are retried with no back-off). The flat polls stay flat as stores arrive; these loops do not. Claims, leases, the run ledger and its alerts are sound. Before opening is the cheapest time to fix the loops and the triggers.

clean: An empty table before opening is not a finding. No feature in this dimension should be retired, parked or hidden because its queue has never held a row; the counts in production are idle cost and the team's own testing.

Most dispatcher jobs are already set-based: one to six statements over all stores, so their idle cost stays the same at 60 or 6,000 stores (read: /home/user/kaizen-store/src/server/kaizen-life-handoffs.ts:502-551 six statements, /home/user/kaizen-store/src/server/sms.ts:691-718, /home/user/kaizen-store/src/server/bonus.ts:550-576 four, /home/user/kaizen-store/src/server/store-trial.ts:79-104 two). Only the per-store loops in CR-3, CR-4, CR-6 and CR-9 grow.

Claims and leases are sound: queues are claimed with 'for update skip locked' and an expiry (30 server files use it; read /home/user/kaizen-store/src/server/broadcasts.ts:465-482, /home/user/kaizen-store/src/server/integrations.ts:1031-1041, /home/user/kaizen-store/src/server/dream-factory.ts:459-474).

The run ledger and its alerts (/home/user/kaizen-store/src/server/cron-runs.ts, /home/user/kaizen-store/src/lib/cron-health.ts) are worth keeping: a late or failing job shows on the platform home and one failing job does not stop the others. Only how often it is written needs changing.

Chromium is imported lazily (/home/user/kaizen-store/src/server/browser.ts:10-16) and traced into seven route patterns only (four with CHROMIUM_FILES, three with DOCUMENT_PDF_FILES, /home/user/kaizen-store/next.config.ts:50-66); an idle run of a Chromium route never loads the browser. The auditor wrote 'four routes'.

Request-side after() is used well: 32 files outside cron kick work the request itself just created (checked: /home/user/kaizen-store/src/server/site-tools.ts:245, /home/user/kaizen-store/src/app/admin/(gated)/[store]/broadcasts/actions.ts:93, /home/user/kaizen-store/src/server/support-inbound.ts:148, /home/user/kaizen-store/src/app/admin/(gated)/[store]/products/actions.ts:118). The store admin layout's two after() checks are one query each when nothing is missing (/home/user/kaizen-store/src/app/admin/(gated)/[store]/layout.tsx:68-73, /home/user/kaizen-store/src/server/connect.ts:257-269 and 539-546).

findings.title: Nine routes are called every minute whether or not anything waits
findings.evidence: pg_cron posts to nine routes every minute: 12,960 calls a day. cron_jobs says they last took 0 to 72 ms; seven answer before working. Idle paths as read: autopilot 13 statements, broadcasts about 15, integrations about 14, theme-shots 8, cookie-scan 3, dream-factory 2, page-jobs, page-looks and pack-pictures 1 each, plus one ledger upsert per route and one for dream-factory.advance: about 68 a minute. integrations runs an update and a delete on integration_deliveries every minute (66,533 calls each in the stats). Most queues are also kicked by the request that fills them (site-tools.ts:245, broadcasts/actions.ts:93, support-inbound.ts:148, triggerLook in page-looks.ts:126-139), so the minute poll is mostly a safety net. Six routes have a true queue (a row waits or it does not): page-jobs, page-looks, pack-pictures, dream-factory, theme-shots, cookie-scan. The other three carry several features with time-derived work (automations, review requests, gift cards, ad conversions; goal reviews and events; support emails, workflows, store events).
findings.cost: 12,960 invocations a day of functions that are already warm (not 12,960 cold starts) and about 97,900 idle statements a day. Each call opens fresh connections to the pooler, because idle ones close after 5 s (db/client.ts:14). In database time it is small: net.http_post totals 3,974 s in 78 days, 51 s a day on average and about 150 s a day at today's schedule (estimate). The function size (47 to 125 MB traced) is paid at deploy and on a cold start, not per call: page-jobs evaluates 10.9 MB of JavaScript at start; the rest is files read only when used. Estimate: the pool rule keeps an instance running about 5 s per call, about 18 instance-hours a day across the nine routes; what Vercel bills for that was not checked. The floor is flat: it does not grow with stores.
findings.who_pays: The server per invocation (Vercel) and the Supabase pooler; the database a little. Its largest measured consequence is the scheduler's log (CR-5).
findings.fix: Keep the routes; change the trigger. Put the 'is anything due?' checks in one SQL function (it can be tested in PGlite; the cron block only runs where pg_cron exists) and let one pg_cron job each minute call only the routes that function names, plus every route every 15 minutes as a sweep. Gates for the six queue routes: page-jobs = page_ai_jobs waiting; page-looks = page_looks queued; pack-pictures = store_starters.pictures_wanted_by set; dream-factory = dream_runs unfinished; theme-shots = a unit waiting or running; cookie-scan = a scan queued (the weekly pick moves to the sweep). For broadcasts, autopilot and integrations a platform-wide gate ('any automation on', 'any autopilot setting', 'any open conversation') is true from the first store that uses the feature, so it only saves until then; their lasting fix is inside the routes (CR-3). Raise the gated routes' everySeconds so cron-health does not call a skipped route late, keep the tick itself in the ledger, and do REL-06's open item here so a ledger row is written only when work ran. This keeps docs/capacity.md:202 (heavy work has a route of its own).
findings.saving: Estimate. Lasting, whatever the store count: the six queue routes fall from 8,640 calls a day to the sweep's 576 plus the minutes with real work, and about 33,000 idle statements a day go. Until the first store uses each feature, the other three routes (4,320 calls, about 64,800 statements a day) are skipped too; after that they run every minute, as they should. pg_cron's own runs fall from 13,250 to about 1,730 a day only with the single tick; the smaller step ('where exists' on each of the nine schedules) still writes nine log rows a minute.
findings.risk: A gate that forgets a kind of due work delays it to the 15-minute sweep; it is never lost. A gated route is cold on its first call after a quiet spell: triggerLook(), where a person waits, then pays a cold start on the 125 MB page-looks function (today the minute ping keeps it warm). Scheduling logic moves into SQL; D263 records that every scheduled call once failed for hours unnoticed, so the gate needs a test and the tick a ledger row. cron-routes.scan.test.ts and the docs that name the schedules (D33, D263, docs/capacity.md:200) change with it.
findings.already_tracked: Partly. The PSI audits advise folding the every-minute routes into one as PERF-10 (docs/audits/psi-2026-10-24.md:146, psi-2026-10-28.md:356, psi-2026-10-31.md:532, psi-2026-11-01.md:788); it never became an item in psi-followups.md. REL-06's item for the seven routes that work after answering is open (psi-followups.md:477).
findings.verify_note: Re-opened every cited file and the schedule; 12,960 calls and the idle counts for autopilot (13), cookie-scan (3), theme-shots (8) and dream-factory (2) hold; broadcasts and integrations read in part. Re-measured the traced sizes from the build (47.3 to 52.7 MB, three at 125.4 MB) and page-jobs' 118 chunks, 10.9 MB. Changed: 'each call loads a function of 47 to 125 MB' is wrong, the function is warm and only 10.9 MB is code evaluated at start; 'a fresh pool per call' is fresh connections, the pool object persists; net.http_post is first by total time but 51 s a day; the 93% saving holds only while nothing is used, so I split it into the six queue routes (lasting) and the three feature routes (until first use); added the cold-start cost to triggerLook and that the one-line step does not shrink the cron log. Whether Vercel packs these routes into shared functions was not checked (no Vercel access in this review).

findings.title: The dispatcher runs all 83 jobs every five minutes: one cadence for everything, one ledger write per job, five connections
findings.evidence: runJobs() starts 78 jobs at once with Promise.all and five more follow, all with EVERY = 300. Nine are pure prunes with retention of 24 hours to 180 days (searches, search cache, forms, docs reads, idempotency keys, OAuth tokens, chat counts, recommendation events, page copies), though docs/capacity.md:112 puts a prune in the daily cron. About 21 more are tied to a day, an hour or a week (the platform briefing at 07:00 Oslo, staff summaries, analytics alerts, report emails, autopilot reports and budgets, nightly translations, legal upkeep and legal sources, business changes, recurring invoices, auto-archive, Instagram, platform books, and houseCustomers, which rebuilds the list of every owner and applicant in one transaction each run and sends it to the database as JSON several times). Every job writes its own ledger row: 84 upserts a run, 565,049 so far on a table of about 100 rows. All of it shares a pool of 5 connections: the run takes 1.3 s while the jobs' recorded times sum to 12.1 s, and the five jobs run one after another at the end took 4 to 7 ms each, so most recorded time is queueing. A query that waits more than 5 s for a connection throws (pg-pool).
findings.cost: At least 248 statements per idle run (auditor's floor, not recounted), about 71,400 a day; small in database time. The real exposure is at opening: 83 jobs queue on 5 connections with a 5 s limit, so one job that holds connections for real work (a store copy, a sync) can make the others fail with a connection timeout. houseCustomers grows with every owner on the platform, every five minutes.
findings.who_pays: The database and the dispatcher's function, every five minutes; later, the jobs that time out behind a busy one.
findings.fix: Give runJobs() a cadence per job (300, 3,600 or 86,400 s), decided from one read of cron_jobs at the start; hourly jobs run in the first five minutes of the hour, as the two existing ones do, so 'at seven in Oslo' still holds. Check each job's promise before slowing it. Keep at five minutes: status, page schedules, cart and SMS reminders, support, follow-ups, hand-offs, the continuations, expiries, tracking, payments, invoices, the accounting syncs, and trials (settleTrials() is the only code that makes a store public again after its owner pays, store-trial.ts:101). Keep the high-churn prunes (chat counts, idempotency keys, OAuth tokens) at five minutes or hourly, or give them a row limit: a daily delete of a busy table can pass the 15 s statement limit and then never succeed. Prefer the cadence over moving jobs into the daily route, which runs everything in one untracked Promise.all. Write the ledger once per run (one multi-row upsert; a failure at once). Run jobs in small groups instead of 78 at once so the pool's 5 s limit is not met.
findings.saving: Estimate: about 8,100 job runs a day fewer from cadence (30 jobs x 288 become about 560), and ledger round trips from 84 to 1 per run (about 24,000 a day fewer). The larger gain is headroom: fewer jobs competing for five connections when real work arrives.
findings.risk: An hourly job that fails is retried an hour later. A job slowed by mistake breaks a promise quietly (trials is the example found). cron-health scales its allowance with every_seconds, so 'late' still works. A ledger written at the end is lost if the function is killed mid-run; the job then reads as late. cron-routes.scan.test.ts:43 pins the literal line of the uiTranslations job in the dispatcher and must follow a new shape.
findings.already_tracked: No. PSI REL-06 (done) made the ledger; the earlier advice to split the dispatcher was answered with maxDuration, not with cadences.
findings.verify_note: Counted the jobs (78 + 5 = 83) and summed the 83 durations in the stats file (12,111 ms, not 12.5 s). Read the nine prunes: all are plain deletes. Read cron-runs.ts, client.ts and pg-pool's index.js:206-225 for the 5 s queue limit, which the auditor did not mention. Changed: 'trials' must not go hourly (reopenAfterPlan has one caller, the job); the daily-or-slower count is about 30, not 31; moving every prune to daily is unsafe for the high-churn tables under the 15 s statement limit; the daily route is not tracked per job, so a cadence in runJobs is the better home. The 163-query floor was not recounted. Whether houseCustomers may lag an hour is a small choice for the team (D467 names the five-minute job but promises no timing).

findings.title: The marketing and autopilot minute routes: 28 idle statements a minute now, and per-store, per-order work every minute once a feature is on
findings.evidence: The auditor's case was that two minute routes and 36 dispatcher jobs poll tables that never held a row. That is true of the statistics and is not a reason to change anything: every feature is unused before opening, and these statements are already counted in CR-1 (28 of its 58) and CR-2 (36 of its 83 jobs). What the same files show, and what will matter, is how the work grows once a feature is used. runAutomations() loads every enabled automation and then, per store and kind, runs one storeById read and one due query, every minute, for emails whose delays count in days. queueAdConversions() re-offers every eligible order of the last seven days to every connected ad platform each minute and relies on 'on conflict do nothing' to drop what is already queued. sendReplyEmails() reads every conversation that is not anonymised, with no status filter, each minute. The autopilot route runs 13 statements a minute, three of them the same 'paused?' read. The dispatcher jobs named by the auditor (hand-offs 6 statements, SMS, bonus 4) are set-based and stay flat.
findings.cost: Today: 28 idle statements a minute, part of CR-1's floor. At opening (estimate from the SQL, not measured): automations cost two statements per store per kind per minute, so 2,000 stores with two automations are about 6,000 statements a minute inside a 50 s budget; ad conversions and support emails cost in proportion to a week of orders and to all kept conversations, not to what is due.
findings.who_pays: The database and the broadcasts and integrations functions, every minute, in proportion to stores and history once the features are used.
findings.fix: Make each of these a set-based 'what is due' statement across all stores, as the other jobs are: one query per automation kind that returns due sends for every store; an anti-join (not exists in ad_conversions, or a marker on the order) in place of re-offering seven days of orders; a 'has an unsent answer' predicate with a partial index for support emails. Read the 'paused?' flag once per route run. Begin each route with one statement that says which of its features has anything due and skip the rest. Do not build a separate platform-wide 'table has a row' switch: it stops saving the day the first store uses a feature.
findings.saving: Estimate: no new saving today beyond CR-1. At opening the routes' cost follows due work instead of stores times kinds and a week of orders; the auditor's '25 jobs skipped each run' would have lasted only until first use.
findings.risk: A welcome email with no delay is expected within a minute or two; keep the minute cadence for it. A set-based due query must keep the per-store plan limit on marketing emails (automations.ts:281-289). Each rewritten statement needs its integration test.
findings.verify_note: Opened every cited file. The autopilot's 13 idle statements and the broadcasts route's order hold, and the 20 dispatcher examples the auditor names do map to tables in the never-used list; I did not recount all 36. Changed: dropped the argument from 'no store has used this' (owner's clarification) and the kind 'speculative'; the cost was double-counted with CR-1 and CR-2; the 'skip while the table is empty' gate saves only before opening, so it is not worth its own step. Rewrote the finding around what the cited code will cost once used: the per-store loop in runAutomations (automations.ts:264-271), the seven-day re-offer in queueAdConversions (ad-conversions.ts:55-68) and the unfiltered conversation read (support-email.ts:92-110). These growth figures are estimates read from the SQL; no plan was run.

findings.title: AI upkeep re-reads whole catalogues, sites and libraries every five minutes to learn nothing changed
findings.evidence: knowledge: for each site with a chat agent on, every run reads the site's locales (2 queries), every published page with its whole 'published' JSON, its blogs and its content entries, compares versions in JavaScript, runs a delete, resolves the AI and reads stale passages. A page that yields no passages gets no version (replacePassages deletes and inserts nothing), so it is cut again on every run: 91,200 'delete from knowledge_chunks where page_id' calls removed 782 rows in all. embeddings: each run joins every active product translation of every store on Kaizena Flow's AI to its terms and hashes title, terms and description in SQL to find stale ones (10,201 calls, 148 s), though a product save already kicks the same work with after(). media: a loop over every store that has media: aiFor, a delete, a select each, and every item goes stale again after a day by design ('so what uses an item is kept current'), which is the 13,414 updates on 468 rows and drives the 'where each picture is used' statement (145 ms mean). altTexts: its first query lists every site with a picture the AI may still describe, then per site resolves the AI and reads the site's languages and due pictures until five sites with work are found. Each aiFor() reads ai_providers (237,563 calls in the stats) and, for a store on the platform's key with a plan limit, sums the month's AI cost.
findings.cost: The dispatcher's four slowest database jobs after the status probes: alt-texts 604 ms, media 555, knowledge 542, embeddings 241. Database time is small today (a few hundred seconds in 78 days) because there are 60 stores. It is the part of scheduled work that grows with stores times pages, products and pictures. Estimate: the embeddings statement takes 14.5 ms for today's few hundred translations; it cannot use an index for 'hash differs', so at a few hundred thousand translations it nears the 15 s statement limit and the job fails each run. The media and knowledge loops run their stores one after another inside the dispatcher's 300 s.
findings.who_pays: The database and the dispatcher every five minutes; it scales with every store that has a chat agent, media or products, used or not.
findings.fix: Find stale rows in SQL and mark them when they change. knowledge: keep the cut version per page (a column or a small table) so the query returns only pages published since, record the version even when a page has no passages, and kick it from the publish action. embeddings: keep the after() kick; make the sweep hourly and per store with a 'changed since' marker (products.updated_at against the vector's) instead of hashing everything. media: keep the reason for the daily re-check but meet it another way: mark a picture stale when a page or product that uses it is saved, or re-check weekly; loop only over owners that have stale rows (one grouped query). altTexts: select only sites with a picture that is actually due, in the first query. Resolve the AI connection once per store per run.
findings.saving: Estimate: the four jobs fall from about 1.9 s of recorded time to a few statements per run; the 91,200 empty transactions and the daily re-touch of every picture stop; cost per store becomes cost per change. Before opening there is no data to migrate, so the version column and markers are cheap to add now.
findings.risk: A missed 'mark stale' leaves a vector or the chat's knowledge out of date until the sweep. Search by meaning and the chat agent are affected, so keep an hourly sweep. The media change replaces a written reason (daily re-check keeps uses current); the marker or a weekly check must cover it.
findings.already_tracked: no (docs/audits/psi-2026-10-24.md:146 judged these 'incremental'; the code and the stats show the knowledge loop and the media re-touch are not)
findings.verify_note: Re-read all four jobs line by line; each claim holds. Confirmed the knowledge re-cut from the code (no insert when a page has no passages, so min(version) stays null) and from the stats (91,200 deletes, 782 rows). Confirmed the product-save kick at products/actions.ts:118. Added what the auditor left out: siteLocales' two queries per site, aiRoomLeft's extra reads per store (ai.ts:217, 235-239), and the statement-limit estimate for embeddings. Raised confidence to high for the evidence; the growth figures are estimates. Under the owner's clarification this is the scheduled-work finding that matters most: it is cost per store, whatever the store uses.

findings.title: pg_cron's own run log is never pruned and is 77% of the database
findings.evidence: pg_cron writes one row to cron.job_run_details for every run and never deletes them. The baseline schedules 14 jobs; two are retention deletes for commerce tables, none for cron's own log. rg for job_run_details and log_run over src, scripts, docs and supabase/migrations finds nothing outside the first draft of this review. Measured in production: the cron schema is 564 MB of a 731 MB database; the app's own schema is 124 MB.
findings.cost: 564 MB today (measured), 77% of the database. It grows by 13,250 rows a day at today's schedule: estimate 8 to 21 MB a day, 3 to 8 GB a year (the row size is not measured; 564 MB over roughly 350,000 rows gives the upper figure).
findings.who_pays: The database: disk, every backup and every restore. It grows with the schedule, not with use.
findings.fix: Add one schedule in a custom migration: a daily 'delete from cron.job_run_details where end_time < now() - interval 7 days'. The disk is given back only by a one-off 'truncate' or 'vacuum full' of that table; the postgres role may not be allowed either on the cron schema, in which case the space is reused and growth simply stops. CR-1's single tick cuts new rows by about 87%.
findings.saving: Up to 564 MB of 731 MB (measured size; how much comes back depends on the truncate or vacuum), and 8 to 21 MB a day of growth stopped (estimate).
findings.risk: Low. The log is only useful for recent debugging; cron_jobs already keeps each job's health. Seven days of history stays.
findings.verify_note: Re-ran the search: no cleanup anywhere. The auditor estimated 190 MB without a measurement; prod-db-stats.md (updated after the audit) now gives the cron schema as 564 MB, so the size is three times the estimate and the confidence is high. Added that a plain delete does not shrink the file, and a growth range labelled as an estimate. The kind 'dead' holds: nothing reads the rows.

findings.title: The cookie scan's due check reads every site every minute without a usable index, and failing sites are retried hourly ahead of healthy ones
findings.evidence: Each minute claimScan() runs two updates and then a statement that lists every open site and, per site, runs two subselects on cookie_scans to find its last scan. Stats: 49,338 calls, 192 s, the fifth most expensive statement; cookie_scans has 1,101,927 sequential scans reading 962 M rows, the most of any table. Less the banner's 70,257 reads that is about 21 scans per call, so the due check explains it (about ten sites, two subselects each). An index on (store_id, created_at) exists (cookie_scans_store_created_idx), but the subselects compare with 'is not distinct from', which Postgres does not serve from a btree index (confirm with EXPLAIN), so each one reads the table. The schedule started 1,796 scans in 34 to 45 days, 40 to 50 a day, where about ten sites scanned weekly would give under two: a failed scan is retried every hour (RETRY_AFTER) with no back-off, and the pick orders by 'done_at nulls first', so a site that has never scanned well is always taken before a healthy site that is due. The route claims one scan per call.
findings.cost: Today: 3 statements a minute and about 4 s of database time a day; 40 to 50 Chromium runs a day, each up to twelve page renders of our own sites. At opening (estimate from the code): the check is sites times scans-per-site every minute, so a few thousand sites means millions of rows read a minute and then the 15 s statement limit; one scan a minute caps the schedule at 1,440 scans a day (about 10,000 sites weekly), and 60 always-failing sites would take every slot and starve the rest.
findings.who_pays: The database every minute; the server and the storefront functions for each scan.
findings.fix: Keep one row per site with its next scan time (or rewrite the subselects with '=' for stores and a separate branch for the platform's null, so the existing index serves them). Back off a failing site: an hour, then a day after three failures, and order the pick so due healthy sites are not behind failing ones. Call the route only when a scan is queued and do the weekly pick in the 15-minute sweep (CR-1). Take more than one scan per run when several wait.
findings.saving: Estimate: the due check from about 21 table scans a minute to one index read every 15 minutes; Chromium runs from 40 to 50 a day to about two at today's size if retries are the cause.
findings.risk: The cause of the extra scans is inferred from the counts (hourly retries); check with one read-only query before changing the retry rule. A longer retry delays a site's first good scan after an outage by up to a day. Templates are scanned on purpose (they are public sites, cookie-scans.ts:90); leave that as it is.
findings.verify_note: Re-read claimScan() and the indexes. The call counts and the 962 M rows hold. Changed: an index on (store_id, created_at) does exist (baseline_3_rules.sql:7591), so 'there is no index' is the wrong diagnosis and 'add the index' alone would not help: the null-safe comparison is what stops its use. The days behind the 1,796 scans are 34 (49,338 calls) to 45 (65,200), so 40 to 50 a day, not exactly 39. Added the ordering that puts failing sites first and the one-scan-a-minute ceiling, both read from the code. Dropped 'leave out sandboxes and templates': templates are included on purpose and I could not confirm sandboxes qualify.

findings.title: The theme-shots route rebuilds its whole wanted list every minute
findings.evidence: runThemeShots() starts each minute with queueThemeShots(): it reads every published theme with its whole snapshot JSON (35,101 calls, 101 s, 348,763 rows, about ten themes a call), the themes' contents, the showcase stores and every theme_shots row (88,341 sequential scans), then one update, a claim under an advisory lock and a prune read: about 8 statements a minute. What is wanted changes only when a platform admin publishes a theme, a version or a demo store, and those three paths already call askForThemeShots() (design-presets.ts:825 and 2368, store-starters.ts:326), as docs/theme-showcase-phase-2.md says.
findings.cost: About 11,500 statements a day and every published theme's snapshot read 1,440 times a day. A fixed floor: themes are the platform's, so it does not grow with stores.
findings.who_pays: The database and the server, every minute.
findings.fix: Take queueThemeShots() out of the start of the minute's run: the publish paths already call it. Keep it in the 15-minute sweep as the safety net, and keep the 'run that stopped' update with the claim. With CR-1's gate the route is not called while no unit waits or runs.
findings.saving: About 8 statements a minute to 0 while idle (about 11,500 a day); the snapshot read falls from 1,440 to at most 96 a day.
findings.risk: A publish path added later that forgets to ask leaves a theme without new photographs for up to 15 minutes, until the sweep.
findings.verify_note: Re-read theme-shots.ts and the route; the statement count and the stats hold. Changed the fix: the auditor proposed adding queue calls to the publish actions, but they are already there (askForThemeShots has three callers), so the work is only to stop the per-minute rebuild. Added that this floor is fixed and does not grow with customers' stores.

findings.title: Kaizena Flow's own payouts are read from Stripe every five minutes
findings.evidence: runPlatformBooks() calls stripe.payouts.list for the last 40 days in every mode that has keys, on every dispatcher run, with no throttle, and upserts every payout it gets back each time. Payouts arrive at most daily. Stores' payouts, by contrast, are read once a day per store through payout_reads. Separately, invoiceJobs() calls ensureSubscriptionEvents for test and live; it remembers the answer only in the instance's memory, so each cold instance asks Stripe for the webhook endpoint again.
findings.cost: 1 to 2 Stripe API calls per run: 288 to 576 a day, whatever happens. Once payouts exist, also one upsert per payout of the last 40 days per run. Up to 2 more Stripe calls per cold start (how often is not known).
findings.who_pays: The server per run, and Kaizena Flow's Stripe rate limit.
findings.fix: Read the platform's payouts once a day with the payout_reads pattern the stores use. Keep 'events checked' in the database with a date instead of in memory.
findings.saving: About 288 to 576 Stripe calls a day to 1 or 2.
findings.risk: A payout is posted to the books up to a day later than now. If the books must show it the same hour, read hourly instead.
findings.verify_note: Re-read the three functions and the stores' pattern; the calls and counts hold. Two edits: the case no longer leans on platform_payouts being empty (it is a cost per run whatever the use), and I removed the alternative 'on Stripe's payout.paid event, which the billing webhook already receives': rg finds no payout event handled in src/server.

findings.title: The invoice job re-asks the same waiting stores every five minutes, with no back-off and no order
findings.evidence: storesWithDocumentWork() returns up to 50 stores that have a paid order of the last 120 days with no invoice, with no 'order by' and no note of why the order waits. The job then calls commerce.issue_waiting_invoices and commerce.issue_missing_credit_notes for each. Stats: 9,909 calls each, 132 s and 35 s (13.3 ms and 3.5 ms a call), and no invoice came of them: the same stores come back on every run. The SQL function already calls issue_missing_credit_notes itself (line 10553), so the job's second call repeats it. The function retries only orders whose reason is 'invoice_failed'; a store waiting for its seller's details is asked again all the same.
findings.cost: About 17 ms of database time per waiting store per run, for up to 120 days per order; 167 s so far. At opening (read from the code): new owners who take orders before filling in their business details will be common; once more than 50 stores wait for a reason that does not clear, a store whose invoice could be issued may never be among the 50 picked.
findings.who_pays: The database every five minutes; later, an owner whose invoice is not issued because the job never reaches the store.
findings.fix: Return only stores with something the job can do now: join the waiting reason, or keep a 'tried at' per store and skip it for a day unless its seller's details changed; order the pick by oldest tried. Drop the job's second call to issue_missing_credit_notes. Run the store's waiting invoices at once when the owner saves the seller's details.
findings.saving: About 9,900 function calls per 78 days at today's size to a few a day, and the 50-store cap stops being a way to starve a store.
findings.risk: A wrong 'skip until' would delay a real invoice; clear it when the store's invoice settings or seller's details change.
findings.verify_note: Re-read invoice-issue.ts and the SQL function. The call counts hold. Changed: the auditor asked the owner whether invoicing is broken because production has paid orders and no invoice; the owner has since said those are the team's own test and demo orders, so that is not a decision for the owner and I set owner_decision to false (one end-to-end invoice drill before opening is still worth doing, since no invoice has yet been issued in production). Added two things read from the code: the duplicate credit-note call and the unordered limit of 50.

findings.title: The docs search index is rewritten row by row on every docs change
findings.evidence: When the deployment's docs fingerprint differs, writeDocsIndex() upserts all rows with 'on conflict do update' and no condition, then deletes rows whose updated_at is older than the transaction. Every row is rewritten even when one article changed; each rewrite recomputes two generated tsvector columns and a trigram text and touches three GIN indexes. The vector is kept when the text hash is the same. Stats: docs_index has 1,845 rows, 49,347 updates, and is the largest table in the schema at 33 MB.
findings.cost: About 1,845 row versions written per docs-changing deploy, with GIN upkeep. How much of the 33 MB is dead space was not measured.
findings.who_pays: The database on each deploy that changes content/docs or the contracts. It is deploy churn; it does not grow with stores or shoppers.
findings.fix: Add 'where docs_index.text_hash is distinct from excluded.text_hash' (plus the metadata columns) to the upsert, and delete by key list instead of by updated_at, since unchanged rows will keep their old time.
findings.saving: Estimate: writes per docs deploy from 1,845 rows to the rows that changed. The table file shrinks only with a 'vacuum full'; a plain vacuum makes the space reusable.
findings.risk: Low; the fingerprint and the per-row hash already exist. A row whose metadata changed but text did not must still be updated, so compare those columns too. The delete must change in the same edit or it would remove every unchanged row.
findings.verify_note: Re-read writeDocsIndex() and the table's indexes; the unconditional upsert and the delete by time hold. Edits: the auditor's 'live data about 13 MB' and 'settles near 13 MB after a vacuum' are unmeasured, and a plain vacuum does not shrink a file, so I removed the figure; added the three GIN indexes and generated columns that make each rewrite dearer. Low priority: a fixed, platform-level cost.

findings.title: An unscheduled PDF route is deployed with Chromium, and a 'finished' backfill is still fed by every copied AI picture
findings.evidence: /api/cron/document-pdfs has no schedule in the migrations and no caller in src: rg for 'document-pdfs' and 'pdfJob' finds the route, comments, docs and tests only. Its own comment and docs/wave-1b-invoices.md:808 say 'schedule it where the five-minute job is scheduled; nothing breaks without it', and nobody did. The scan test excuses it as 'run by the dispatcher's invoice job and by staff', which the code does not do. It traces to 101.9 MB with Chromium. Two tests pin its existence (document-readers.test.ts:121 and 134). aiPictureMarks: its comment and psi-followups call it a backfill done on 31 October, but it is still fed: copyToLibrary() copies an AI picture's row with made_by and without ai_marked_at (media-library.ts:272-277), and templates, themes, home takes and store copies all use it, so every new store that starts from a theme with AI pictures gives the job rows; for each it downloads the picture and its small copy from storage to find the mark already there. secretRotation returns before any query unless a rotation is under way but still writes a ledger row; runJobs() deletes the one retired job's row on every run.
findings.cost: One 101.9 MB function in every deploy that nothing calls, and waiting PDFs are made only on first download although 'Try again' says the job makes them on its next run. aiPictureMarks: one query a run today; at opening, two storage downloads per copied AI picture, ten pictures a run, for nothing. The rest is two statements a run.
findings.who_pays: The build and deploy (function size); the dispatcher and storage per new store; an owner waiting for a PDF.
findings.fix: document-pdfs: schedule it behind CR-1's gate (a document with no PDF) so the promise in 'Try again' is kept, or delete the route with its tracing entry and correct the two tests and the scan test's reason; either way make the scan test's reason true. aiPictureMarks: make copyToLibrary() carry ai_marked_at over, then take the job out of the dispatcher and add it to RETIRED_JOBS once 'ai_marked_at is null' is empty. Leave keepStripeWebhooksCurrent at five minutes: it is one read of a four-row table, and it is what brings Stripe's events back after a change of address. The ledger write for a job with nothing to check goes away with CR-2's single write; delete retired rows once, in a migration.
findings.saving: One Chromium function out of the deploy or put to use; the storage downloads for copied AI pictures never start; about 290 job runs and 288 deletes a day.
findings.risk: Retiring aiPictureMarks before the copy carries the mark would leave new rows unmarked in the table for good (the files themselves keep their mark, being byte copies). Deleting the route without the tests fails CI.
findings.already_tracked: no (psi-followups.md:216 marks the backfill done but does not retire the job; docs/audits/psi-2026-10-28.md:383 notes document-pdfs as unscheduled)
findings.verify_note: Re-ran the searches and opened each file. The orphaned route holds (101.9 MB re-measured), and I found the two tests that pin it, which the auditor missed. Changed: aiPictureMarks is not finished. copyToLibrary() (six callers) inserts AI pictures without ai_marked_at, so the job keeps getting rows and will get more with every new store; retiring it as proposed would be wrong without the one-line fix to the copy. Refuted the sub-item 'run keepStripeWebhooksCurrent daily': the saving is 288 one-row reads a day and the risk is up to a day of lost Stripe events after a domain change, the incident the job was written for. The auditor's '1,150 pointless job runs a day' becomes about 290.

findings.title: The daily job is scheduled twice, at the same minute
findings.evidence: vercel.json schedules /api/cron/subscription-reminders at '0 7 * * *' and pg_cron schedules the same route at '0 7 * * *'. The route's comment says this is meant: 'Supabase's scheduler calls it (D33), and Vercel Cron too where CRON_SECRET is set; each reminder goes once whoever calls.' That was written when the route sent reminders; it now runs about 39 functions in one Promise.all (24 prunes, erasures, currency rates, domain renewals). Whether CRON_SECRET is set in Vercel, and so whether the second call runs or is answered 401, was not checked (no Vercel access in this review).
findings.cost: If the secret is set: the whole daily job runs twice at the same moment every day, on five connections each. If not: one refused call a day. Either way the second schedule adds a second scheduler to reason about.
findings.who_pays: The server and the database once a day; and anyone debugging a daily job that ran twice.
findings.fix: Remove the crons block from vercel.json and keep pg_cron as the one scheduler (D33, D263), or keep Vercel's as a deliberate fallback an hour later and say so in the route's comment. cron-health already reports the daily job as late after 30 hours.
findings.saving: At most one duplicate run of the daily job a day; one scheduler instead of two.
findings.risk: If pg_cron stops, Vercel's call no longer covers the daily job; the ledger's alert would say so within 30 hours.
findings.verify_note: Re-opened vercel.json, the schedule, the route comment and cron-auth.ts: both schedules exist at the same minute and the route accepts either secret. The double call is documented as intended for the reminders, which the auditor quoted; what has changed since is how much else the route now does. Counted 24 prune calls and about 39 functions in the route. The effect in production stays unconfirmed, so confidence stays medium.

findings.title: Status checks are kept raw for 91 days though the page shows one bar a day
findings.evidence: Each run inserts one row per measured part (five of the six today): 1,440 rows a day. The prune keeps 91 days, so the table heads for about 131,000 rows; it has 20,547 after about 14 days. The page's read groups all 90 days into per-day counts and also runs a 'distinct on (component)' over the whole table with no time bound, each time its cache is refilled, and the dispatcher refreshes that cache every five minutes. So far: 1,072 sequential scans reading 10.5 M rows. Only two reads need raw rows: the newest check per part, and seven days of timings for the Dublin measurement.
findings.cost: Estimate at steady state: about 131,000 rows and 20 MB, and two reads of the whole table on each cache refill. A fixed platform cost; it does not grow with stores.
findings.who_pays: The database, and a visitor to /status after each five-minute refresh.
findings.fix: Keep a small table of per-day, per-part counts that the job upserts (ok and total), read the page from it, and keep raw checks for 8 days. A smaller first step: bound the 'newest check' read to the last day so it uses the (component, checked_at) index.
findings.saving: Estimate: about 131,000 rows to about 11,500 raw rows plus 540 day rows; the page's read from 131,000 rows to about 550.
findings.risk: Low. The SLO minutes are computed from day counts already (dayBars), so the numbers stay the same. A new table needs its migration, its row-security line and its place in the personal-data register.
findings.verify_note: Re-read the insert, the prune, the page's two reads and the index. Numbers hold: 20,547 rows over 1,440 a day is 14.3 days; six parts are listed and five are measured. Added the unbounded 'distinct on' read, which the auditor did not single out, and a smaller first step. Low priority: bounded and platform-level.

findings.title: Nothing limits or measures scheduled work, so each feature adds a poll
findings.evidence: The scan test asks only that a cron route has a maxDuration and is tracked. The written rule ('new heavy work gets a route of its own') has produced nine every-minute routes, from six on 24 October; each PSI audit since has noted it under PERF-10 and none stopped it. A new job is one line in runJobs() with no cadence, no due check and no reason. The ledger cannot show idle cost or growth: for the seven routes that work after answering it records 0 to 1 ms (the answer only), and for dispatcher jobs it records time spent waiting for one of five connections (sum 12.1 s against a 1.3 s run). No check asks whether a job's work is per store or set-based, which is how the loops of CR-3, CR-4, CR-6 and CR-9 got in. The dispatcher's description is one comment line of 4,212 characters in a 24 KB route file, repeated by the inline comments.
findings.cost: Unbounded growth: 83 jobs now, and nobody sees which ones will cost per store. An agent reading the dispatcher pays about 6,000 tokens for the file (estimate from 24,495 bytes).
findings.who_pays: Everyone later: the database, the server, and each agent session that opens these files.
findings.fix: Make a small registry the dispatcher and the tick both read: for each job its name, cadence (300, 3,600, 86,400), its due check and a one-line reason, and whether it is set-based or loops over stores (a loop needs a cap and an order). A scan test fails a job without them and fails a new every-minute schedule without a gate. Record in the ledger whether a run found work and how many rows it handled, and show idle runs and per-store loops on Usage and limits. Replace the long comment with the registry.
findings.saving: No direct saving; it keeps CR-1 to CR-4 from growing back and turns the next audit into a query instead of a code read.
findings.risk: Low. The registry must not become a second place to forget: generate the runJobs() list from it. cron-routes.scan.test.ts:43 pins one job's literal line and must follow.
findings.already_tracked: Partly: REL-06's open item (psi-followups.md:477) covers recording the after-answer routes' real work; PERF-10 in the PSI audits names the growth; no plan sets a cadence, a gate or a budget.
findings.verify_note: Re-read the scan test, the rule in capacity.md and the dispatcher's header; measured the comment line (4,212 characters) and the file (24,495 bytes); the PSI audits do say six routes on 24 October and note the growth on each later date. Edits: the sum of durations is 12.1 s, and I added the missing check that matters most after the owner's clarification: nothing asks whether a job's work is per store.
